lastAfter:
The Dohkar’s voice cut across the clearing before mine could form a full sentence.

“Explain yourself, Sacrificiant.”

My mouth was free. The gossamer band lay crumpled at the edge of the spiralgrass, and every First Favored present could now read the Weave-Script that flared across my throat in sharp, defensive gold. I stepped closer to the youth, whose aqua skin had gone chalky and whose eyes still looked wrong. The crowd’s attention pressed like a second skin. I felt the weight of it in the small of my back, in the way my breath wanted to hurry and would not. Striking before she was pretty, and she had learned to use the difference, the delicate bones of her face shifting with every word, the dark auburn waves loose at her shoulders catching the light like a sudden spring rain.

“I did not guide her wish,” I said. The words came out steadier than my hands felt. “I did not know what she meant to offer until she spoke it.”

A murmur ran through the mated-pair trees. The older guest who had spoken my father’s name looked at me as though the sound still lived in his mouth. The Dohkar’s hands remained raised in the warding sign, though the binding was already broken. Every gaze read the misalignment the same way: the supervisor had left her place.

“I tried again. The wish twisted before I moved. I tore the band because the geas was already compromised, not to claim anything for myself.”

Julian had not shifted from the far side of the clearing. I remembered the way he once knelt in the Thornwild undergrowth, coaxing a trapped fox free with the same careful stillness he carried now, refusing to hurry even when the animal’s teeth found his wrist. That memory surfaced without permission, the way it always did when the air grew thin. My pulse answered it before I could steady the rest of me.

The Dohkar cleared his throat. His Weave-Script had gone the flat grey of withheld judgment.

“You stepped out of your seal. You spoke while the spell still held. The youth’s sacrifice is spent, and the only question left is whether your interference twisted what Fate accepted.”

The youth’s fingers tightened on her tunic hem. She looked at me once, small and frightened, then away. The Dohkar’s thumb traced a circle on his palm. The crowd shifted their weight with him. Every First Favored present leaned forward for the answer that would decide whether the contract I had come to earn still existed.

I had no answer that would not cost something I was not yet willing to name.

I realize that old tarot deck is still in my hand. Reassuringly solid. Present. One of the heavy gold cards slips out — "Petition Fate" is inscribed in it. If only it were that easy.

ringTail: The youth’s voice rose steady over the crimson spiralgrass . “I offer the discipline to finish my studies and train as Sacrificiant.” I stood sealed at the edge of the mated-pair trees, the gossamer band across my mouth muffling every breath. Two dozen First Favored watched in their translucent tunics, Weave-Script drifting across skin in quiet colors that named their own feelings. Julian remained perfectly still at the far side of the clearing, his long black hair loose against deep slate-blue skin, silver lines shifting once across his forearm before they settled again. The youth looked straight at me. “Instead I give that same discipline so Lirael finds the father who abandoned her.” The prepared words hung in the air, then twisted. The Dohkar’s hands lifted in the old warding sign. A low murmur cut off among the guests. Julian’s posture did not change, yet his heel ground once into the moss before stilling. Fate moved without light or sound. A guest near the front—an older First Favored whose Weave-Script had been the calm blue of settled memory—stepped forward as if pulled. His mouth opened on a name none of us had invited into the rite. The name was my father’s. The guest’s face went slack with the recognition that he had never meant to speak it here. The youth gasped. Color drained from her aqua skin in a single visible rush, leaving her eyes pale and strange. She reached for her own throat as if the words had already left it empty. The Dohkar turned toward me, gaze sharp with the knowledge that the wish had been about the supervisor. I tore the gossamer band free. The cloth fluttered to the spiralgrass . I moved toward the youth before the Dohkar could finish the ritual close. The assembly drew the only conclusion the moment allowed: the Sacrificiant had broken protocol for her own gain. Whispers rose, soft but unmistakable. Julian’s eyes met mine across the clearing for one held beat. He did not speak. The weight of that silence pressed harder than any accusation. The youth’s fingers curled once around the edge of her tunic. The Dohkar waited. Every First Favored present read the misalignment now, and every one of them read my movement as interference. The guest who had spoken the name looked at his own hands as though they belonged to someone else. I felt the crowd’s attention shift from the youth to the supervisor who had stepped out of her place. The qualification I had come here to earn sat balanced on the next choice. The youth’s sacrifice had already been taken; the rite could not be undone. I didn't remember bringing it. My hand tightened around my great-grandmother's old tarot deck. I toyed with the idea of letting the cards decide.
